source: Cullen, Fan, van der Brugge & Elga (2018) Improving analytical reasoning and argument understanding: a quasi-experimental field study of argument visualization
finding: Independent (Princeton, not the Melbourne group) test of argument-diagram training. A 12-week seminar on diagramming real philosophy texts beat controls on LSAT logical reasoning and on blind-graded essays.
numbers: Seminar N=105 (2013-2017, seven courses of 15), control N=56. LSAT: seminar +2.6 items (SD 2.8), d=0.77 pre to post; control +0.48 (SD 3.2), d=0.11 n.s.; difference in gain d=0.71, 95% CI [0.37, 1.04], t(159)=4.3. Pretest control 17.4 vs seminar 15.9 (d=0.27, n.s.). Essays (seminar 15, control 44): d=0.87, CI [0.26, 1.48]; structure d=0.76, accuracy d=0.74, understanding d=0.97.
quote: Seminar students improved substantially more on LSAT Logical Reasoning test forms than did control students (d = 0.71
limits: Quasi-experiment, no randomisation; controls were students who wanted the seminar but lacked space. Seminar included weekly individual feedback, so diagramming and feedback are confounded. Essay sample small (15 vs 44). Humans, not LLMs.
agent_relevance: Closes the 0.70 SD figure for a non-Melbourne group: the effect on a hard transfer test is real but about 0.7 SD, not 0.8, and comes with feedback. Supports 'make the structure explicit' as a teaching move; does not transfer directly to an LLM.

source: Cullen et al. (2018), discussion of prior argument-visualisation studies (citing Thomason et al. and van Gelder's handbook chapter)
finding: Cullen et al. say earlier argument-mapping studies mostly had no control group and used the CCTST. In recent studies that gave both tests, effect sizes were three times smaller on LSAT than on CCTST, with only slight LSAT gains. They blame the CCTST's weak psychometrics (low internal consistency, non-equivalent forms, repeated items).
numbers: Ratio 3:1 (CCTST vs LSAT effect) as reported secondhand from Thomason et al.; no raw numbers given in this paper.
limits: Secondhand: Thomason et al., Twardy 2004, Alvarez 2007 and van Gelder 2015 were NOT opened (paywalled or not found). The 0.34 and 0.8 SD figures in earlier lines remain unreconciled at the primary level.
agent_relevance: The headline 0.8 SD depends on the test used. Any claim that mapping 'improves reasoning' must name the outcome measure. Keep K24 contested.

source: Kim & Yang (2026) TRACE: Toulmin-based Reasoning Assessment through Constructive Elements for LLM CoT Evaluation (ICML 2026)
finding: Labels each sentence of a model's chain of thought with Toulmin and metacognitive roles (claim, evidence, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal, monitor) and scores the flow. The score tracks accuracy and, used as an RL reward, beat an accuracy+length reward.
numbers: 26,320 reasoning blocks, 7 models, 39 benchmarks. Pearson r=0.741 between mean TRACE and accuracy (n=273 model-benchmark pairs); per-model r 0.81 to 0.91 (qwen-flash 0.914). Labeller DeBERTa-v3-base: human kappa 0.672 (400 sentences), macro F1 0.666. GRPO on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: GSM8K 74.75 (SFT base), 77.86 (acc+length), 84.69 (+TRACE); ARC-Challenge 55.80, 57.93, 59.90.
limits: Correlation is across models and benchmarks, so model size confounds it. One RL run, no seeds or CIs seen; 1.5B model only. Measures structure of reasoning, not factual correctness (authors say so). Not a test of restating the input argument.
agent_relevance: First measured link between Toulmin-shaped reasoning and downstream accuracy at comparable length. Partly addresses gap 1 for the model's own reasoning, not for restating a given claim. Suggests a cheap structural check on the agent's trace.

source: Zhan et al. (2026) From Answers to Arguments: Toulmin-Guided Curriculum Goal-Conditioned Learning for clinical diagnosis
finding: Training LLMs to write diagnoses in Toulmin form (data, rebuttal of alternatives, warrant, backing, qualifier) raises a Toulmin-quality score a lot but accuracy only to the level of plain SFT or RL.
numbers: MedCaseReasoning, Llama-3.1-8B: Vanilla acc 22.46; SFT-CoT 32.14 (TrustScore 60.86); SFT-CGCL(stage 3) 30.07 (70.92); GRPO 32.83 (73.24); CGCL 32.67 (72.89). Llama-3.2-3B: SFT-CoT 28.33 (59.91); CGCL 28.90 (71.35). Clinician check: T-Eval vs clinician Spearman 0.74, ICC(2,k)=0.63. Stage 3 added 4.52 TrustScore points.
limits: Accuracy is itself an LLM-rubric claim score, not exact match. T-Eval is judged by LLMs and built by the same authors. Toulmin structure is the trained target, so the quality gain is partly by construction.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 10 and gap 1 in part: Toulmin format gives more inspectable, better-structured output, but no accuracy gain over plain CoT SFT (32.14 vs 32.67 on 8B). Use structure for audit and faithfulness, not as an accuracy lever.

source: Bhargava, Tonelli et al. (2026) Have You Been Convinced? NARS neuro-symbolic argumentation reasoning on ChangeMyView
finding: LLM-built bipolar argument graphs plus gradual semantics predict persuasion (delta) a little above chance. Zero-shot reasoning LLMs given the same argument structure stay at or below chance.
numbers: Best NARS F1=0.57, AUC=0.56 (alpha=0.3; ensemble F1 0.5682). Random acc .5025, F1 .5266, AUC .5. Logistic regression AUC .5869. Qwen3.6:27B zero-shot F1 .2525, AUC .5227; with structure F1 .2647, AUC .5140. GPT-oss:20B F1 .1341 to .1639 with structure. Bootstrap CIs about +-0.05 to 0.06.
limits: Weak task (labels are delta events), tiny margin over random, wide CIs overlapping across configs. Graphs are LLM-derived, not gold. LLM baselines are point estimates.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gaps 3 and 1: handing an LLM the extracted structure gave only marginal gains (F1 +0.012 and +0.030). The structure label is not obviously a lever for the answering model.

source: Baba & Chudziak (2026) From Argument Components to Graphs: Multi-Agent Debate with Confidence Gating for Argument Relations (KES 2026)
finding: Attack links are the weak class. Debate on only the uncertain pairs lifts attack F1 a little; debating everything gives almost no net gain. Fine-tuned RoBERTa nearly misses attack.
numbers: UKP essays v2, 2,407 test pairs, 42 attack instances. Macro F1: manager alone .562; gated (confidence under 0.70, 14% = 332 pairs debated) .585; full debate .561. Attack F1: .383 manager alone, .427 gated, .378 full debate, .374 at threshold 0.75 (48% debated). At 0.70: 84 predictions fixed, 48 broken (net +36); full debate 249 fixed vs 236 broken. RoBERTa-base attack F1 .071, RoBERTa-large .167 (160 attack training pairs).
limits: Single corpus, gold component boundaries assumed, margin over best baseline (.585 vs .578) not tested for significance, only 42 attack test cases so each flip moves F1. No false-attack rate reported.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 6: a selective second pass raises attack F1 by about 0.04 at 14% of the calls, but a blanket counter-argument pass adds noise. Low attack recall is partly class imbalance for trained models. Gate the 'find the attack' pass on low confidence.

source: Baba & Chudziak (2026) On the LLM Verification for Argument Graph Generation
finding: Tests an LLM reviewer against a plain deterministic validator on argument graphs with injected defects. The reviewer finds almost all defects but also rejects good graphs and changes its verdict on identical input.
numbers: 112 arg-microtexts graphs (576 statements, 385 arguments, 63 undercutters); one defect per graph per class. LLM reviewer (Gemini 3.7 Flash, temp 0.1) recall: missing field .96 (unstable .04), duplicate id 1.00, dangling ref 1.00, support cycle .97 (70 graphs). On 112 correct graphs: objects to 9.8%, verdict flips on identical input 6.2%, median latency 2,758 ms vs 1 ms for the validator (0% false objections).
limits: One LLM, one corpus, synthetic structural defects. Says nothing about semantic mistakes in a restatement.
agent_relevance: Relevant to gap 3: schema-level checks on a restated argument (every premise has a source span, no cycles, no orphan nodes) should be done by code, not by asking the model again. Supports a deterministic check after S2.

source: Castagna et al. (2024) Critical-Questions-of-Thought, limitations and ablation sections
finding: Re-read for gap 5. The paper has no sample-and-vote or equal-token baseline and no non-LLM judge. It lists multiple sampling only as something that could be added on top. An ablation using only plan (step 1) and final answer (step 4) already beats the standard baseline.
numbers: 20 separate tests (CQoT vs baseline and vs CoT, 2 domains, 5 models): CQoT best in 18, joint best in 1, CoT beat it on Nemotron-51B reasoning. Judge is GPT-4o, with the reference answer re-prompted when the judge misread it. Generation settings list max new tokens 2000 for the baseline setup and 8192 for the pipeline setup.
limits: Token budget differs between arms. Gap 5 therefore stays open: no source found that runs CQoT against majority vote at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Do not credit the critical questions alone. Any trial in our agent must include a token-matched plain CoT arm and a self-consistency arm.

source: Calvo Figueras & Agerri (2025) Benchmarking Critical Questions Generation: A Challenging Reasoning Task for LLMs
finding: Critical questions from Walton-style schemes are hard for LLMs to generate well. Reference-based LLM judging tracks human ranks better than plain similarity.
numbers: About 5K manually annotated questions; 11 LLMs zero-shot; no model produces more than 57% Useful questions on average; Useful share is 67.46% in validation references but 42.68% in the test set (806 questions). Judge agreement with human labels: STS_reference IAA 0.57; judge ranking vs shared-task human ranking Pearson 0.86 (Claude) and 0.80 (Gemma). Best open model gemma-2-27b-it 54.03.
limits: Evaluates question generation, not whether asking the questions helps an answer. Judges disagree on which model wins (gpt-4o vs claude-3-5-sonnet vs Qwen2.5-VL-72B).
agent_relevance: Context for gaps 5 and 10: the critical-question step itself is unreliable (under 57% useful), so a CQoT gain may depend on a few good questions. Measure question usefulness in our own test.

source: Feng & Hunter (2026) Making Implicit Premises Explicit in Logical Understanding of Enthymemes
finding: Re-opened for gap 2: the step-count effect is tested only on two entailment benchmarks (ANLI, ARCT), 1 to 3 steps, one engine (DeepSeek v3.2), choosing between two fixed candidate premises. Not tested on math, planning or code.
numbers: 250 entailment items per setting. ANLI accuracy none/original/1/2/3 steps: .496/.520/.624/.660/.716. ARCT: .276/.292/.480/.496/.560. Best F1 class 1 on ARCT: original .21, 1-step .45, 2-step .52, 3-step .58. Pool shuffled with seed 1129; 150 valid rows per class.
limits: Authors say it is not unrestricted generation and not state of the art. Fixed candidates, thresholds (m, c) tuned per step type, one author group. The 4-step peak and 5-step drop are from a different paper (Microtext), same group.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: the 3 to 4 step peak is not shown on non-benchmark tasks or across engines. Gains here come with an AMR plus SAT checker, so the benefit is of premises plus a formal check, not of premises alone.

source: Freedman et al. (2026) Neurosymbolic Learning for Inference-Time Argumentation (ITA)
finding: Forcing a verdict to be computed from generated, scored arguments (quantitative bipolar framework) costs little against direct prediction but is not better. Direct-prediction baselines are strong.
numbers: Qwen3-8B, two ternary claim-verification sets (TFU accuracy, AVeriTeC balanced accuracy). Per the text, SFT is best on TFU and direct GRPO best on AVeriTeC among non-argumentative baselines; ITA beats untrained argumentative baselines and is described as competitive. Table 1 text was column-scrambled in the PDF, so exact per-row values were not extracted.
limits: Exact values not extracted; judged only from the authors' wording. One 8B model.
agent_relevance: Supports 'structure for faithfulness, not accuracy' (with d04, d05). A verdict computed from explicit grounds is inspectable but did not beat direct label prediction.

source: Tran et al. (2026) LLM-INSTRUCT at UZH Shared Task 2026: Constraint-Aware Retrieval and Selective Debate for Paragraph-Level Argument Mining
finding: Winning shared-task system using only open models up to 8B. Key design: shrink the label space before generation and debate only uncertain cases. Rare labels stay near zero.
numbers: 141 tags; ranked 1st overall, 1st in F1, 5th in LLM-judge. Subset ablation: removing retrieved examples cut recall 22.76 to 16.68 and F1 by 5.17 points; removing the per-dimension cap changed F1 40.26 to 39.84 and false positives 3,529 to 3,575. Tags with at most 5 references: F1 only 2.51%. Gold relation labels were not released, so only rank positions are reported.
limits: No gold relation precision available. Paragraph-level UN text. Exact leaderboard scores not published.
agent_relevance: Constrain the output vocabulary of the restatement (fixed role labels, closed relation set) and escalate only uncertain items. Relation prediction beyond the head labels remains weak.

source: Verma et al. (2026) Towards Full-Text Scholarly Argument Mining using Entity-Anchored Claim Extraction
finding: On long papers, anchoring claims to named scientific entities lets the task be done sentence by sentence, avoiding long-range linking. Encoders trained on LLM-ensemble silver labels beat those trained on the small human gold set.
numbers: 50 sentiment-analysis papers; human gold Krippendorff alpha 0.80, 113 claim-bearing sentences of 300 candidates, 199 structured claim records; silver set 1,487 claims by majority vote of an LLM ensemble.
limits: Single domain (NLP sentiment papers); claim extraction only, not premise-conclusion links. Gold set is small.
agent_relevance: Bears on gap 9 (long text): the workable route for long inputs was chunking into sentence-level units with an anchor, not one global restatement. No direct measure of a length cliff was found.

source: Henselmans, Prinzhorn & Libert (2026) Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis: Can Model Reasoning Withstand Scrutiny?
finding: Probes nine frontier models with Walton-scheme critical questions and Govier cogency criteria on 200 high-ambiguity moral items. Failures cluster on grounds and sufficiency, and the argument scheme used in the justification differs from the one used in the reasoning for about 20% of dilemmas.
numbers: 9 models, 200 MoralChoice items, 6,778 judge-scored cells, 89.6% inter-judge agreement on the binary failure judgment. Reasoning defended better than post-hoc justification on every model and every dimension.
limits: Moral dilemmas, LLM judges, no gold. Not an accuracy study.
agent_relevance: Indirect evidence for gap 10. A restatement made after the answer may not match the reasoning that produced it, so restate first (S1/S2) and answer after.

source: Search record, 3 Nov 2026: arXiv listing searches for adversarial ARCT, warrant, Toulmin-correctness and premise-count studies with current LLMs
finding: Negative result. The arXiv search for 'argument reasoning comprehension' returned only 4 papers (Habernal 2017, Niven and Kao 2019, two SemEval-2018 system papers). No paper was found that scores a current LLM on the adversarial ARCT set, or measures whether Toulmin parts are correct, not only present. Searches 'ARCT warrant GPT', 'Toulmin warrant backing LLM generate evaluate' and 'argument structure prompting restate' returned no results.
numbers: 4 hits for ARCT; 10 hits for 'Toulmin LLM' (TRACE, CGCL, CQoT among them, none testing correctness of parts); 16 hits for 'argument structure LLM reasoning'.
limits: arXiv only. The shared WebSearch budget was exhausted, and Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the arXiv API were rate-limited (429), so venue papers may exist that this search missed.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 10 stay open. Treat the ARCT 79% LLM score as unverified for cue use; plan to run the adversarial set ourselves.

source: Gorur, Rago & Toni (2025) Argumentatively Coherent Judgmental Forecasting
finding: Dropping forecasts whose stated reasoning conflicts with the forecast raises accuracy for both people and LLMs (abstract and introduction read; per-metric tables not extracted). Crowd user studies show people do not by themselves follow the coherence property.
numbers: Abstract: filtering incoherent predictions improves forecasting accuracy consistently for human and LLM forecasters. Exact Brier values not extracted in this session.
limits: Forecasting with debate frameworks, not single-agent restatement. Same group as earlier a14/b14/b15 (counted once). Numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Weak support that checking claim-reason coherence helps at decision time; the check is a filter after the fact, not the restating step.
